The same patients measured **three or more times** (before surgery, then at 6 weeks, 3 months and 1 year), or **matched sets** of three or more patients. This is [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd) extended past two measurements. As on [page 8](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd), each test asks one question first: **does the outcome differ anywhere among the visits (or groups)?** [Which visits differ?](#which-groups-differ) explains what to do next.

::: {.callout-note}
## 💡 How every section on this page works
Each section answers one question about one of the practice's datasets: the joint replacement PROMs and matched sets, or the boot vs cast trial from [page 6](06-two-unpaired-groups.qmd#unpaired-t). Its first code block loads the packages and the data, so you can jump straight to the section you need. Run that section's blocks in order, top to bottom.

To keep the code short, the joint replacement examples use every case, including both cases of patients who had both sides operated on (80 patients in the whole cohort; [page 2](../foundations/02-demographics.qmd#setup) counts them). In a real study, decide how to handle them ([page 3](../foundations/03-distributions.qmd#paired)) and say what you did.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: these tests drop anyone with a missed visit
Repeated-measures ANOVA, the Friedman test and Cochran's Q need every patient measured at **every** visit. A patient who missed one visit is dropped completely, along with their other measurements. Below, 574 procedures had a pre-op PROMIS physical function score, but only 328 had all four, so the analysis loses 574 − 328 = 246 procedures (246 ÷ 574 = 43%); the first section counts them. If the patients who miss visits differ from those who don't, the result is biased. [Mixed models](../beyond/16-mixed-models.qmd#why-mixed-models) use everyone's available data, and are usually the better choice for repeated PROMs.
:::

## Repeated-measures ANOVA {#repeated-measures-anova}

**The question:** Does physical function (PROMIS-29+2) change over the first year after surgery?

### When to use it

- A **measurement** taken **three or more times** on the same patients (or once on each member of a matched set).
- The changes between visits are roughly normal, or there are plenty of patients.
- **Sphericity:** the spread of the changes is similar for every pair of visits. Mauchly's test checks it; if it fails, the **Greenhouse-Geisser** correction adjusts the [degrees of freedom](../glossary.qmd#degrees-of-freedom){.term}. Both programs below report both.
- Only patients measured at **every** visit are included (see the warning above).
- If the outcome is [skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term}, bounded or ordinal → the [Friedman test](#friedman).

PROMIS physical function is a T-score: 50 is the average of the US general population. The four-question form in PROMIS-29+2 runs from 22.5 to 57.0, and 57.0 is the best it can record.

### What the test really does

Repeated-measures ANOVA is a [one-way ANOVA](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#one-way-anova) that first sets aside the differences between patients.

1. Work out the [mean](../glossary.qmd#mean){.term} of each visit, and each patient's own mean over all the visits.
2. Split the variation in the scores into three parts. **Between the visits:** how far the visit means are from the overall mean. **Between the patients:** how far each patient's own mean is from the overall mean. **Left over:** how much each patient's scores still bounce around once the visit means and that patient's own level are taken into account.
3. Set the part between the patients aside. Some patients score high at every visit and others low, and that says nothing about change over time.
4. Divide each of the other two parts by its [degrees of freedom](../glossary.qmd#degrees-of-freedom){.term}, then divide the results: **F = variation between the visits ÷ variation left over**. If the scores didn't change over time, F would be close to 1. The larger F, the smaller the [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

Setting the differences between patients aside is what makes the test sensitive: each patient serves as their own comparison, as in the [paired t test](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#paired-t). Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds F by hand.

### Read the output

- **F = 326.1, with 3 and 981 degrees of freedom** (DFn/DFd in R, DF in Python): how much the visit means differ, compared with how much each procedure's scores bounce around their own average. 3 = four visits minus one; 981 = 3 × (328 procedures − 1).
- **p** (R prints `7.55e-147`; pingouin's table rounds it to `0.0` in the `p_unc` row): far below 0.001. `e-147` is [scientific notation](../glossary.qmd#scientific-notation){.term}: the decimal point moves 147 places to the left.
- **Mauchly's test, W = 0.995, p = 0.903** (`W_spher` and `p_spher` in Python, which sums them up as `sphericity True`): no evidence that sphericity is violated, so the uncorrected result stands.
- **Sphericity corrections** (R) or **eps** and **p_GG_corr** (Python): the Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon is 0.997 (1 means perfect sphericity), and the corrected p-value is still far below 0.001. `HFe` and the `[HF]` columns in R are a second correction, Huynh-Feldt; you can ignore them here.
- **pes = 0.499** (R) or **np2** (Python): partial eta squared, below.

### Effect size and 95% CI

**Partial eta squared (η²~p~)** is the share of the within-patient variation that the visits account for. As a rough guide, 0.01 is small, 0.06 medium and 0.14 large. **Generalized eta squared** (ges = 0.417 in R) also counts the differences *between* patients, which makes it comparable with designs that aren't repeated measures; report it when readers will compare studies of different designs.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

effectsize::eta_squared(pf_model, partial = TRUE)                         # with a 95% CI

### How to report it

> **Methods:** PROMIS-29+2 physical function T-scores across the four visits were compared with one-way repeated-measures ANOVA in patients with all four measurements. Sphericity was assessed with Mauchly's test, with the Greenhouse-Geisser correction planned if it was violated. Partial eta squared (η²~p~) is reported as the effect size.
>
> **Results:** Of 574 procedures with a pre-op PROMIS physical function score, 328 had all four measurements. Their mean T-score was 36.1 (SD 5.4) before surgery, 39.4 (SD 5.5) at 6 weeks, 44.9 (SD 5.5) at 3 months and 48.2 (SD 5.6) at 1 year (F(3, 981) = 326.1, p < 0.001; η²~p~ = 0.50, one-sided 95% CI 0.47 to 1.00; Mauchly's test of sphericity p = 0.903).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: a significant F doesn't say which visits differ
The ANOVA says the visit means aren't all the same. To say *when*, compare the visits with paired tests and a correction for multiple comparisons ([page 15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-repeated-measures-anova)). And remember who's missing: the patients behind the 246 procedures without complete data may have recovered differently.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: which tools check sphericity
- **R:** base `aov(... + Error(case_id / visit))` gives the same F test but ignores sphericity; `rstatix::anova_test()` adds Mauchly's test and the corrections. rstatix rounds its numbers to 3 decimals.
- **Python:** pingouin's `rm_anova(correction=True)` reports Mauchly's test and the Greenhouse-Geisser correction. statsmodels' `AnovaRM` gives the F test only.
- **Effect sizes:** pingouin returns either partial (`effsize="np2"`) or generalized (`effsize="ng2"`) eta squared; rstatix returns both if asked.
:::

## Friedman test {#friedman}

**The question:** With a removable boot, does the EFAS score keep changing between 6 weeks, 3 months and 12 months?

### When to use it

- An outcome measured **three or more times** on the same patients, when it's **[skewed](../glossary.qmd#skewed){.term}**, **ordinal** or has a **[ceiling or floor](../glossary.qmd#ceiling-effect){.term}**. The EFAS score adds up six questions, and by 12 months scores crowd toward its maximum of 24.
- It ranks each patient's own scores (1st, 2nd, 3rd) and asks whether some visits tend to rank higher than others.
- Only patients measured at **every** visit are included.
- If the outcome is a roughly normal measurement → [repeated-measures ANOVA](#repeated-measures-anova).

### What the test really does

The Friedman test compares the visits inside each patient, using only the order of that patient's own scores.

1. Take one patient at a time and give their scores a [rank](../glossary.qmd#rank){.term} across the visits: 1 for the lowest, 2 for the next and 3 for the highest. Tied scores share the average of their ranks.
2. Work out the **mean rank** of each visit across all the patients.
3. If the scores didn't change between visits, each visit would be equally likely to get any rank, and every visit's mean rank would be close to 2, the middle of 1, 2 and 3.
4. The [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term} measures how far the visits' mean ranks are from that middle value. The further they are, the smaller the [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

Because each patient is ranked separately, it doesn't matter that some patients score high at every visit and others low. Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds the statistic by hand.

## Cochran's Q test {#cochran-q}

**The question:** Does walking-aid use change over the first year after surgery?

### When to use it

- A **yes/no** outcome measured **three or more times** on the same patients (or once on each member of a matched set).
- It extends [McNemar's test](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#mcnemar) to more than two visits, and, like McNemar's, it only learns from patients whose answer changed.
- Only patients measured at **every** visit are included.

### What the test really does

Cochran's Q compares how many patients answer yes at each visit, within the same patients.

1. Count the yes answers at each visit.
2. Count each patient's yes answers across the visits. A patient who answers yes at every visit, or no at every visit, says nothing about change and drops out of the calculation.
3. If nothing changed over time, each of a patient's yes answers would be equally likely to fall on any visit, so the visit totals would come out about equal.
4. The [test statistic](../glossary.qmd#test-statistic){.term}, **Q**, measures how unequal the visit totals are, compared with how unequal chance alone would make them. The larger Q, the smaller the [p-value](../glossary.qmd#p-value){.term}.

With only two visits, Q is the statistic of [McNemar's test](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#mcnemar) without its continuity correction. Once the test has run, a box under "Read the output" rebuilds Q by hand.

## Stratified Cox regression {#stratified-cox}

**The question:** In sets of three patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, does the risk of revision differ between implants A, B and C?

### When to use it

- The outcome is **time until an event**, and the patients come in **matched sets** of three or more.
- A Cox model **stratified** by matched set compares the implants only **within** sets, as on [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#stratified-cox), which used just the A and C patients from the same sets.
- With few events, expect wide CIs. [Page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd) covers Cox regression in full.

### What the test really does

A stratified Cox model works like the Cox model on [page 8](08-three-plus-unmatched.qmd#cox), with one change: every comparison stays inside a matched set.

1. Take one matched set at a time and follow its three patients forward from surgery.
2. Each time one of them is revised, look at which members of the set were still being followed just before: the patients [at risk](../glossary.qmd#at-risk){.term} in that set.
3. If the implants carried the same risk, the revision would be equally likely to happen to any of those members. The model tries out values for each implant's [hazard ratio](../glossary.qmd#hazard-ratio){.term} and keeps the values under which the revisions that really happened, taken together, were most likely.
4. A revision tells the model nothing if no other member of the set was still being followed, and neither does a set with no revision at all.

The patients in a set are alike in the factors they were matched on, so those factors can't explain a difference between the implants. Once the model has run, a box under "Read the output" works out the observed and expected revisions inside the sets by hand.

### Effect size and 95% CI

The **hazard ratios** with their 95% CIs: within matched sets, implant C carried about four times the hazard of revision of implant A (3.91, 95% CI 1.28 to 11.95). The estimate for implant B (0.43, 95% CI 0.08 to 2.25) is too imprecise to interpret.

### How to report it

> **Methods:** Revision risk was compared between implants in matched sets using Cox regression stratified by set, with implant A as the reference.
>
> **Results:** In 52 sets of three patients matched on procedure, age, sex, BMI and ASA class, the hazard ratio for revision compared with implant A was 3.91 (95% CI 1.28 to 11.95) for implant C and 0.43 (95% CI 0.08 to 2.25) for implant B (likelihood ratio test for implant type, χ² = 13.5, df = 2, p = 0.001).

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Watch out: only 24 events
A Cox model needs events, not just patients. With 24 revisions across three implants, the CIs are wide and the model can't support adjustment for anything else. [Page 14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd#choosing-covariates) covers how many events a model needs.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🔀 R vs Python: strata and convergence
As on [page 7](07-two-paired-groups.qmd#stratified-cox), R puts `strata(set_id)` in the formula while lifelines takes `strata=["set_id"]`. Here lifelines' default convergence matches R exactly; with page 7's pairs it stopped a little early and needed `fit_options={"precision": 1e-9}`. If the two programs disagree in the fourth decimal, tighten it.
:::

## Which visits differ? {#which-groups-differ}

Each test above answers "is there any difference among the visits (or implants)?". When the answer is yes, the next question is which pairs differ. Comparing every pair with an ordinary paired test inflates the chance of a false positive: four visits make six pairs.

| After | Use | Page |
|---|---|---|
| Repeated-measures ANOVA | Paired t tests with Holm's adjustment | [15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-repeated-measures-anova) |
| Friedman | Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank (or Conover) tests with Holm's adjustment | [15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-friedman) |
| Cochran's Q | Pairwise McNemar tests with Holm's adjustment | [15](../beyond/15-post-hoc.qmd#after-cochran-q) |
| Stratified Cox | Hazard ratios against a chosen reference | [14](../survival/14-cox-regression.qmd) |

For repeated PROMs, a [mixed model](../beyond/16-mixed-models.qmd#why-mixed-models) answers both questions at once (does the score change, and at which visits?) while keeping patients who missed a visit.
